speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today, March 9, is Commonwealth Day, which has particular significance this year for Canada.
In October, in your own City, Sir, of Vancouver, we will host the next meeting of the Commonwealth Heads of Government. In that same internationalist tradition, Canada will welcome the second Francophone Summit to Quebec City in September. These are both family meetings for Canada, taking us back to the roots and traditions which shaped our unique country, but also, as strong and vital families, helping us reach
out to new influence and new opportunities in a changing world.
It was once the style to be nostalgic about the Commonwealth. Today, it is one of the most relevant and effective associations to which Canada belongs. Under its auspices we are involved in ocean development in the Caribbean and the South Pacific; in technical co-operation in Asia and in Africa; in scholarships and research on all six continents; in cooperation at Geneva on international trade; and continuing dialogue among countries whose conditions range from the poorest to the most advanced.
In Chittagong, in Bangladesh, last month, I met a Canadian who had been involved in the first Canadian project under the Colombo Plan. That was the beginning of our program of external aid and the beginning also of Canada's reputation in the developing world as a trusted, modern power.

Mr. Speaker, in the past two years, Canada has used the forum provided by the Commonwealth to exercise effective pressure against the evil of apartheid in South Africa. I would like to take this opportunity, on Commonwealth Day, to report to Parliament on recent conversations the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) had in Africa, on my own meetings with some of our Commonwealth partners in Great Britain and Asia, and on consultations held by the Minister for External Relations (Mrs. Landry) and the Minister of State (Immigration) (Mr. Weiner) with representatives of several South African countries.
Canada played a very active role in launching the activities of the Eminent Persons Group and drafting the first set of Commonwealth sanctions against South Africa. We have applied every sanction and every measure approved by the Commonwealth in Nassau and London. In fact, the Prime Minister is playing a major role in this respect among Commonwealth leaders, both personally and as chairman of the Vancouver meeting.
It was in this spirit that in January at Victoria Falls, he met with the leaders of three Commonwealth countries, members of the front line States: President Kaunda of Zambia, Prime Minister Mugabe of Zimbabwe and President Masire of Botswana. He saw for himself the potential danger that the violence inherent in apartheid represents for fragile economies. From all sides, people voiced their concern that increasing violence as a result of South African intransigence and aggression would lead more and more victims of apartheid to give up ail hope for a negotiated settlement.

March 9, 1987
Statements by Ministers
The Prime Minister reiterated Canada's commitment, expressed in the following terms on October 23, 1985 at the United Nations, and I quote:
Canada is prepared, if there are no fundamental changes in South Africa, to consider sweeping sanctions against that country and its repressive regime. If there is no progress in dismantling apartheid, we may have no alternative but to break off completely our relations with South Africa.

The front line states understand that Canada does not seek, through sanctions, to bring the South African Government to its knees, only to its senses. Our approach is steadily to build international pressure on South Africa as we restrict its trade. Canada will invoke further measures when we consider that they will have the most impact. We have told the front line leaders that we think that for them being on the front line itself means economic sacrifice and political risks. They should not be held to a rigid timetable on the questions of sanctions, costly as they would be to them and vulnerable as they are to South African retaliation.
In the Nassau Accord the Commonwealth has called for a suspension of violence on all sides. Our Commonwealth partners in the front line states understand Canada's position that we cannot support violence, although we can understand the feelings of those who have felt the full effect of the violence of apartheid. Indeed, part of the Prime Minister's (Mr. Mulroney) purpose in going directly to the front line states was to demonstrate again that they are not alone in this fight against apartheid, or in their work to build and to maintain their own economies.
Canada is determined to provide material as well as moral support to South Africa's neighbours. At Victoria Falls, the Prime Minister signed an agreement to build a $50 million electrical interconnecter line which will permit Botswana to tap into the electrical resources of Zimbabwe and Zambia. This is only one of many ways in which Canada is helping South Africa s neighbours to reduce their vulnerability to South African sanctions. Over the next five years, we expect to contribute approximately $30 million annually to the South Africa Development Co-ordination Conference, SADCC. That is in addition to the $400 million we will be providing in bilateral assistance to southern Africa over the same period. In New Delhi, I discussed with Prime Minister Gandhi means by which Canada might work closely with the Fund for Africa, established by the non-aligned movement, particularly in the work of ensuring secure transportation routes. The Minister of State for Immigration (Mr. Weiner) was in Botswana for the most recent SADCC meeting, and discussed similar projects.
At the same time, we have been working to assist the victims of apartheid in South Africa. In the current year, $1.5 million is being disbursed for assistance to the families of political detainees, and we have mounted a $7 million education program. Nine days ago, in Montreal, Dr. Alan Boesak
suggested to me other ways in which Canadian humanitarian help could be effective in South Africa.
The Prime Minister of Canada is the only leader of an Economic Summit country to have been to southern Africa since the pressure for change has built against apartheid. He has discussed the issue regularly with our Summit partners, and will put the question on the agenda of the Venice Summit.
Since the African National Congress plays such a major role now in South Africa, and will be closely involved in any resolution of that problem, the Prime Minister and I look forward to meetings with the President of the African National Congress, Oliver Tambo, in the next few months. Mr. Terence Bacon, our former High Commissioner to Zambia and Zimbabwe, has been seconded to the Commonwealth Secretary-General as special adviser on southern Africa.
As was noted last week in the Standing Committee on Human Rights of the House, by the New Democratic Party Member for Windsor-Walkerville (Mr. McCurdy), the issue of the fight against apartheid has risen above normal partisan considerations in Canada. It is a common commitment of this Parliament and country.
In a broader sense, so is our commitment to the Commonwealth. What was once a connection to our past has now also become a principal instrument of contemporary policy, and a symbol of the breadth of spirit, and the breadth of alliances, which this special country Canada will require to achieve our interests in the future.

Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the Official Opposition, I wish to join with the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) in this recognition of Commonwealth Day, and underline the importance that this day presents to Canadians because of the major responsibility and obligation that the Commonwealth increasingly has to deal with the issues of great concern to people around the world.
We are pleased with, and so register, the opportunity that Canadians will have to see the Commonwealth in action as it holds its major meeting here in October. I am sure that all parliamentarians will find the occasion of Canada hosting that very important meeting to be one that we hope will focus more clearly on Canadian positions on the South African issue. In that manner, it will become not just a matter of bi-partisan support, but a matter of clear commitment by all Canadians of the actions that must be taken.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs has stated that the Commonwealth has now been brought under the front stage of world events. I think that the Secretary of State for External Affairs is correct in saying that. The value of that organization as a way of bringing countries with a wide variety of points of view together is one that we can only see now in its clearest and most honest evaluation that such organizations are of incredible value in today's world. There are not many like them with that particular type of composition.
March 9, 1987

As we saw at the last meeting in Nassau, it provides an opportunity for initiatives to be taken. The question that must be asked is what will be the initiative that is taken at the Commonwealth meeting in Vancouver in October? Quite clearly, we are faced with the tragic failure of the Eminent Persons Group which we all regret, because we certainly supported that initiative. It is clear that the Government of South Africa had no intention of responding to that initiative, and I think that events would show that since that initiative it has undertaken even further Draconian actions, and the further detainment of people. The last figure or estimate is that close to 20,000 people, both black and white, in South Africa are under detention by that Government. The restriction of freedom of the press, perhaps one of the most fundamental freedoms, gives even further cause for anguish.
We should not underestimate the importance and the difficulty which that meeting will face. It is only six months away,and on behalf of our group I wish to urge that some careful planning and policy-making be initiated, so that the developments of the Commonwealth meeting will have the proper anticipation and development leading up to it.
We were encouraged by the meetings taken by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) in his tour of southern Africa, and the efforts made to establish clear communication with the front line states, and with other African states. I believe that our leader has said that we applaud the Prime Minister for that initiative. However, what we raise as a question is the continuing ambiguity that seems to be apparent in the Government's position on the issue of sanctions itself.
During his meetings in Senegal, the Prime Minister stated, and I quote from his words, that "The Commonwealth Summit Meeting will be the determining factor in announcing a complete sanctions package". That sets a very clear timetable. However, last week when the Secretary of State for External Affairs was before the Standing Committee on Human Rights and the same question was asked, we certainly detected less of a willingness to commit to that type of statement made by the Prime Minister.
One thing that cannot be afforded in this most important of all foreign policy initiatives of the Government is any sign of ambiguity or confusion. If Canada is to take the lead in the Commonwealth, as it should, and as it has the opportunity to do, it is absolutely essential that there should be no hesitation or doubt as to where we stand, and what we will do about it.
I wish to use this occasion to urge the Secretary of State for External Affairs to take that into account, and to understand the commitment made by the Prime Minister in his statements in Senegal, and in other places in South Africa. These statements were reported in Canada with eight-inch headlines, that Canada was prepared to undertake full, total, comprehensive economic and diplomatic sanctions. If we now begin to draw away or back away from that position, it will weaken our possibility to provide the strength of purpose and direction that will be required in October.
Statements by Ministers
One of the ways that the Government could clearly signal that there is no hesitation on its part is to now begin the type of discussion and development with those areas of the Canadian business community that are presently engaged in economic relations with South Africa as to what would be required for a total sanction package; how will we go about the disinvestment, how will we go about applying total sanctions? If there is to be any clear signal given, then by demonstrating that we have a blueprint, that we know how we will do it, I think we will strengthen our position, and give strong and undeniable messages to those who need to receive the messages.
I agree with what the Secretary of State for External Affairs said last week in the Human Rights Committee, that one of the primary roles for Canada to play is not only in initiating actions for our own purposes, but in trying to influence the actions of others, of the United States, certainly Great Britain, and members of the European Economic Community. By Canada initiating action now, putting in place the building blocks toward a full sanctions package, it would provide the strength of that message to these important allies and convince them to do the same. We have already had the example of the U.S. Congress substantially overriding the position of the administration in this regard. There are certainly signs that members of the EEC are now prepared to begin that kind of plan.

I urge the Government to provide, perhaps in honour of Commonwealth Day, the kinds of steps we can take domestically to show that we mean business when we get to the meeting in October. I want to make clear that that in no way takes away from what I accept as being the unequivocal commitment of the Government. However, I want to see that commitment followed by action. The action itself should become as important as the commitment in sending out the kinds of messages we want to send. We hope that the meeting in October will provide the platform on which a wide variety of countries can take a further step toward ending apartheid and toward presenting to the world a set of proposals on how that anguished country might move toward a democratic system. If Canada plays its proper role at the Commonwealth Summit in October, hopefully the next time we celebrate this very important day it will be in more positive terms.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I am most pleased to have been chosen by my Party to join with the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) in speaking in recognition of Commonwealth Day.
The Commonwealth, to those not a part of it, must seem a curious institution. Created by conquest, it has become a model of international co-operation based upon the shared values of justice and equality among a diversity of peoples around the globe. Transcending race, transcending religion,

March 9, 1987
Committee Reports
and transcending cultures, it has taught Canadians that our own nation can develop strength and vigour through diversity.
As we have become a multicultural and multiracial nation and have demonstrated our commitment to independence, selfdetermination, economic development, and to the end of oppression and racism, Canada has assumed a position of leadership in this most friendly of international associations and in the world. It has been most particularly in the fight against apartheid that Canada has established a position of leadership within the Commonwealth, displacing even the mother country as its Government struggles to understand that justice is not equivocal or to be delayed.
As noted by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, the people of Canada and the Parliament of Canada see the issue of apartheid as a question, not of partisanship but of justice. All of us support the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) when he said, "if there are not fundamental changes in South Africa, we are prepared to invoice total sanctions against that country and its repressive regime. If there is no progress in the dismantling of apartheid, our relations with South Africa may have to be severed absolutely".
We are concerned, however, that the promised action has been so long delayed. The South African regime has become not less oppressive but more oppressive; not more conciliatory, but more recalcitrant. Thousands have been displaced from their homes in ruthless pursuit of the still existing homelands policy. Thousands more have been jailed, tortured, and killed, including very small children, under the present state of emergency. Devious manipulation of a tortured people has turned black against black, as a curtain of darkness imposed by the evil regime keeps from the world the dark details of its evil oppression.
Even as we applaud the Government's international leadership we must mention, as the Secretary of State for External Affairs failed to do, that Canadians expect more, as was so clearly demonstrated just nine days ago in a meeting of groups opposed to apartheid in Montreal.
As stated in the reports of the Special Joint Committee on Canada's International Relations and the House Committee on Human Rights, they want full legislative, mandatory, universal, economic sanctions imposed against South Africa, and they want them now.
We share, as my colleague in the Liberal Party shares, the concept that Canada must act to demonstrate leadership and to provide a model of what others should do. It has been our consistent position that we exhibit an appropriate model when we exhibit leadership, by applying what most can be done by the country. We have hesitated too long in doing what we can do and should do. I know the Secretary of State for External Affairs has within his vest pocket permission from the Cabinet to proceed with increased sanctions. It is the position of my Party and most Canadians that he should proceed now, so that when the Commonwealth meets in Vancouver in the fall Canada can exercise its leadership, having demonstrated what
should be done by others, most particularly what should be done by the mother country.
I am most pleased, as I am sure are other Members of the House, that the Government, through its Prime Minister, has made a commitment for increased aid to the front line states, for they will suffer, as he has indicated, most of all by acts of retaliation by a South African regime already engaged in actions to destabilize those nations. I hope the Secretary of State for External Affairs has expressed the full commitment of his Government when he was asked last week at the committee hearing whether the Government was prepared, in co-operation with other nations, to provide those means to the front line states by which they may protect themselves against South African aggression, those very establishments we have helped fund to enhance their transportation facilities and to allow their economic growth and development. It will do no good if we give them aid for development while we sit idly by and watch an aggressive military regime undermine our contribution.
We should not forget in that context our commitment to the freedom of Namibia. We should take conspicuous note of the inconsistency involved in our efforts in the front line states, while the United States of America provides $100 million for South Africa's allies in undermining the Angola regime and in resisting the freedom of Namibia.
We join together with all Parties in expressing our national commitment to justice, particularly justice for the South African majority population. However, along with other Canadians, we hope we will not hesitate any longer in expressing the leadership for which so many have called in leading the fight against apartheid.
Hear, hear!

subtopic: PRESENTATION OF FOURTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
PRESENTATION OF FOURTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to present the fourth report of the Standing Committee on Public Accounts. This report deals with the management of Indian bands and moneys.
In a 1984 decision involving the surrender of Indian bands, the Supreme Court of Canada held that the Department of Indian Affairs had a fiduciary duty to Indian people and awarded damages of $11.7 million to an Indian band. Approximately 100 other lawsuits against the Crown are pending, and 25 per cent of these claims with a dollar value represent a potential liability of $1.77 billion. The remainder have no stated dollar value.
The Standing Committee on Public Accounts believes that Indian people should receive the same standard of asset care that all Canadians would expect from a professional trustee. In
March 9, 1987

addition, the Department must protect the Crown from future legal liabilities.
The committee has noted a number of areas where the Department has not met professional standards in the management of lands, estates, and moneys. The Department has indicated three types of responses to these deficiencies which will be monitored closely by the committee.

speechtext:
1.	Was a 10 per cent tariff on English language books imposed by the Government on June 6, 1986 and, if so, to date, what was the total amount collected?

speakeroldname: Hon. Elmer M. MacKay (Minister of National Revenue):
subsubtopic: TARIFF ON ENGLISH LANGUAGE BOOKS
speechtext:
1. Effective June 6, 1986, the Customs Duty on Books Remission Order (1982), which allowed duty free entry of certain books, was revoked. Consequently, novels, works of fiction, some periodicals, publications to encourage enrollment in educational institutions outside of Canada and books of printed music reverted to being subject to the legislated duty at the rate of 10 per cent ad valorem under the most favoured nation tariff and the U.K. and Ireland tariff.

books for the promotion of medicine, the fine arts, law, science, technical training and the study of languages, are not affected by this change and remain duty free.
The amount of duty collected from June 6, 1986 to November 30, 1986 (date of the latest available statistics) was $11,142,000.

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom Hockin (for the Minister of Finance) moved
subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1986-87 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
that Bill C-40, an Act to provide borrowing authority, be read the second time and referred to a Legislative Committee.
He said: Madam Speaker, I rise today to seek approval of Bill C-40, an Act to provide borrowing authority. As Hon. Members are aware, the Financial Administration Act requires that statutory borrowing authority must be obtained from Parliament in order for the Government to borrow. Specifically Part IV, Section 36 of that Act requires that:
No money shall be borrowed or security issued by or on behalf of Her Majesty without the authority of Parliament.
This refers to new money only, rather than the refinancing of existing debt. Under Section 38 of the Act, there is continuing authority to borrow funds to repay maturing debt. While Section 39 provides for short-term temporary borrowing, statutory borrowing authority must be obtained from Parliament to permit the Government to implement a regular debt program to meet its financial requirements.
March 9, 1987

There can be no doubt that the timing of the Bill before us is appropriate. The Government is following the pattern for an improved budgetary process that was set out in a paper the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) tabled in May 1985. The same pattern was followed with the last borrowing authority Bill. One of the suggestions presented in that paper which the Government has been actively pursuing is that parliamentary approval of borrowing authority for each upcoming fiscal year should be sought at the same time as the Budget is presented. The logic behind the proposal was that the Budget presentation in February would set out the financial information for the new fiscal year for parliamentary study. This is a course of action now being taken and I would hope that debate on the Budget and the fiscal stance presented by the Government will be helpful in examining this borrowing authority Bill.

Allow me now to give you a few details concerning the provisions of the Bill and the reasons why this borrowing authority is being sought.

The largest amount is $24.3 billion in borrowing authority requested for the next fiscal year, 1987-88, as set out in Part II of the Bill. I will discuss that in more detail later in my remarks. First, however, I would like to deal with the circumstances underlying the request in the Bill for supplementary borrowing authority in the current fiscal year which ends March 31.
Part I, Clause 2(1), seeks supplementary borrowing authority for 1986-87 of $3.6 billion. This amount is equal to the amount of borrowing authority that has already been used to acquire U.S. dollar reserves during the period from April 1, 1986, to January 31, 1987. While the Government does have a non-lapsing reserve of $2 billion carried forward from borrowing authority legislation in 1984-85, this reserve is not sufficient.

The Government therefore is seeking to borrow an additional amount of $3.6 billion to replenish this $2 billion reserve and have the operating margin required to react on the exchange market when further interventions become necessary between now and the end of this fiscal year.

Clause 2(2) of the Bill provides for the cancellation on March 31, 1987, of all borrowing authority conferred by the above Section that remains unused in this fiscal year 1986-87 and to the extent that it exceeds borrowing pursuant to Section 39 of the Financial Administration Act undertaken between February 18 and April 1, 1987.

Hon. Members know that Section 39 empowers the Governor in Council to borrow when it appears that there will not be
Borrowing Authority
enough money in the Consolidated Revenue Fund to make expenditures.

This action is designed for short-term, temporary use only. The term of the borrowing may not exceed six months and each borrowing requires approval by the Governor in Council.
Financial requirements are seasonally high in the first quarter of a new fiscal year, especially in April when they typically exceed what can be financed through a feasible borrowing operation in that one-month period. Thus, fiscal 1986-87 year-end cash balances will have to be built up in order to help meet these heavy seasonal requirements and this will be done on a temporary basis through short-term borrowings pursuant to Section 39 of the Financial Administration Act.
The Minister of Finance announced on February 26 that authority under Section 39 was being used to provide for a net increase of up to $600 million in Treasury bill borrowings this week. Funds borrowed under this Section cannot be rolled over in the regular way as under Section 38 and will require new borrowing authority. Thus the Bill provides for borrowing authority to the extent it equals money borrowed under Section 39 in 1986-87 to be carried forward into 1987-88 to roll over the maturing debt issued to build up cash balances in the current fiscal year.
The primary reason for seeking supplementary borrowing authority now is the impact on the Government's borrowing operations arising from the recent volatility in the exchange markets which has been quite extreme. Our actions to maintain an orderly exchange market in this volatile environment, in the face of upward pressure on the value of the Canadian dollar during January and early February, have resulted in a very substantial increase in the Government's official reserves. Domestic borrowing was therefore increased to obtain Canadian dollars to finance this increase in reserves. There no longer remains sufficient borrowing authority to facilitate additional borrowings. As a result, the Government found it necessary to use Section 39 of the Financial Administration Act to enable it to continue its debt operations, and I should note that Section 39 was used in similar circumstances in 1983 and 1985.
It is most important that the Government be in a position to maintain an orderly, ongoing debt program so as to rebuild its cash balances. Speedy passage of this Bill will help to achieve this objective and will reduce the need for heavy reliance on short-term borrowings pursuant to Section 39 of the Financial Administration Act.

Now, Madam Speaker, allow me to tell you about the borrowing authority we will need for the next fiscal year. Part II of the Bill provides borrowing authority of $24.3 billion for the year 1987-88. This amount covers the $21.3 billion financial requirements set forth in the Budget plus a $3 billion non-lapsing reserve for unforeseen outlays, including a new

March 9, 1987
Borrowing Authority
build-up of international official reserves during the year 1987-88.

In light of recent exchange market developments, the $3 billion reserve amount being sought is appropriate. In the month of January alone, about $2.5 billion in borrowing authority was used as a result of exchange market operations. The proposed $3 billion reserve will provide the Government with the ongoing flexibility that is needed to rebuild its cash balances.

If I may, Madam Speaker, for your information I should like to table a document explaining the source and use of the borrowing authority for this fiscal year until February 28 1987.	'

One of the fundamental principles of fiscal policy as set out by the Minister of Finance is that the Government should ensure substantial year-over-year reductions in the Government's financial requirements. This is of particular interest to the House because, over three years, the Government will have reduced financial requirements by 28.5 per cent: from $29.8 billion in the year we took office to $21.3 billion in this coming fiscal year. This steady reduction in the demands made by the Government on the nation's savings is one of the most important factors underlying our steady economic advance.
In conclusion, the borrowing authority requested by this Bill is reasonable in the circumstances. The added flexibility we are seeking allows us to cope with sudden large demands for funds and to moderate exchange market fluctuations. It is, I submit, a prudent measure in light of the potential volatility of the exchange markets. The authority we are seeking to cover next fiscal year's financial requirements reflects the Government's ongoing policy to bring about steady and substantial reductions year by year in the federal Budget deficit.
[DOT] (M50)

Ever since this Government took office, the Minister of Finance has clearly expressed our determination to stay within the bounds of financial responsibility. In the context of that policy I urge the House to pass the Bill.
IMr. Raymond Garneau (Laval-des-Rapides): Madam Speaker, in speaking to Bill C-40, our normal reaction might be that the Budget Speech has been read, the Main Estimates have been tabled and that the debate on the Budget Speech is extensive enough to warrant keeping our comments on the borrowing authority Bill to a minimum. However, I think we would not be doing our duty as the Official Opposition if we were to give such short shrift to a Bill that will add to the national debt as much as $30 billion, if we consider the borrowing authority being sought by the Minister in clause (2), that is, $3.6 billion between now and March 31, 1987, the $24.3 billion for current expenditures and a contingency fund of $3 billion, something for a rainy day, but $3 billion just the
same. This Bill seeks borrowing authority for all these amounts.
As I said before, we could go back to what we said in our speech in response to the Budget Speech made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), but I think we should dig a little deeper and put this borrowing program into perspective, in the light of the commitments made by this Government during the 1984 election campaign and also in the light of what was said by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Minister of Finance during the weeks and months following the 1984 election, statements that have been repeated many times both in and outside the House.
Madam Speaker, the group of which I am a member believes it is essential that public administrators act prudently when administering the affairs of this country. We believe in fiscal responsibility, and I may remind the House of what was said by the Leader of my Party, now the Leader of the Official Opposition, in the weeks preceding the election campaign, and of my own comments on financial matters. We have explained many times why, during the 1984 election campaign, the Liberal Party of Canada limited the number of promises and the commitments it made. It was because of a financial situation that was largely the result of an economic recession that had affected not only Canada but the entire western world. The impact of this economic recession has been compared with that of the Depression in the thirties, and if its impact was not as dramatic, this was undoubtedly because of our social programs that helped maintain the purchasing power of Canadians and ward off disaster from many Canadian families.
In other words, throughout the 1984 election campaign we took a position favouring fiscal responsibility not only in words but in actions as well, and I am referring to the kind of limited election program we were advocating. We on this side of the House and the Leader of the Liberal Party who was then Prime Minister, myself and many of my colleagues reminded Canadians of this harsh reality. During that time the Conservatives travelled throughout the country making promises. We counted roughly 330 of them, all rather an expensive drain on the public treasury. Yet at the same time as they were making election promises right and left they also told Canadian consumers they would get new funds through various programs or projects, they were told the deficit would be reduced because it had become imperative to gain control over the public debt. A very conservative approach, quite contradictory of course! One day they were making promises, the day after they were saying they would do this and that. I have had opportunities to debate this issue with many people as it often happens during election campaign, open debates before student groups and various associations, and my experience has always been the same. In the same breath the Conservatives were saying: We will give more and spend less. Altogether contradictory.
March 9, 1987

As 1 have done in earlier debates, Madam Speaker, we might recall the statements made by the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance concerning the solemn commitment that a Conservative Government would not raise taxes. It was imperative not to raise taxes. We were even told that it would be against the economic well-being of all Canadians. So what have we seen since their Party took over? Taxes have gone up dramatically. If we look at tax increases for the years 1984-85, 1985-86 and 1986-87, we find that personal income tax will have increased by 53 percent during that period because of the combined effects of income tax increases brought about by deindexation of tax tables, rate increases, withdrawal of benefits, and so on. Individual taxes, that is personal income tax and taxes on consumer products, will have increased by 53 percent while corporate taxes, including income tax and taxes paid by oil companies, will have decreased by 18 percent. Individuals will pay 53 percent more and corporations 18 percent less.
Madam Speaker, there are two possibilities. Either the Conservatives made promises that they knew they could not keep, which would have been a very petty political game, or else they did not know what it meant to govern the country. I still do not know which is true, but one thing is certain, and that is that this Government has not only neglected to keep its electoral promises, but has also done the opposite of what it had said it would do. It is one thing to promise a bridge and quite another to destroy a bridge. In this case, not only has the Government not kept its promises, but it has done exactly the opposite of what it said, namely brought about a very large tax increase.
Madam Speaker, does this increase, especially in individual income tax and consumer taxes, do these increases of billions of dollars ... The 53 percent tax increase within a three-year period which I mentioned earlier means an increase of $22 billion, or nearly $1,000 for each man, woman, child and senior citizen in Canada. There are new taxes. If we consider the fact that a very large number of people, such as children, pay no taxes, it means that the Mulroney-Wilson Budgets of the Conservative Government will put an additional burden of nearly $2,000 on each Canadian family even though we had been promised lower taxes.
Madam Speaker, it is not surprising that the popularity of a Government which fails so flagrantly to keep its electoral commitments would fall to 22 percent in Canada as a whole. Only 22 percent of Canadians still have confidence in this Government, and the figure is as low as 18 percent in Quebec. This is not surprising since the Government has failed to keep all its commitments.
I said earlier that taxes had been increased even though the Government had said that this would not occur. What effect has this had on the budgetary deficit after three years of a Conservative Government since, according to the Conservatives, the deficit was to be their main priority after the elections? The 1986-1987 deficit keeps to practically the same level as in 1983-1984 when this Government came to power,
Borrowing Authority
that is for the last full year of the previous administration. After increasing taxes by $22 billion, they now come up with more or less the same level of deficit.
And looking now at the impact on the national debt, Madam Speaker, the debt increased to a level where at the end of the fiscal year under review in the estimates and the Budget Speech, this Tory Government will have added $10,000 to the debt burden of each Canadian man and woman, an absolute record for any Government over such a short period of time! In brief, not only did they not honour their commitments with regard to income tax, not only did they just about fail to alter the deficit to any extent, Madam Speaker, we are now coming to a situation where the national debt has increased from $16,000 to $26,000 because of this Tory Government's management.
Madam Speaker, with this legislation we are to all intents and purposes requested to approve a possible $30.9 billion in total borrowings. But, essentially, this Tory Government has succeeded in concealing part of its deficit. This they did in a tricky way in their dealings with businesses. You know how things go-businesses pay out wages and salaries, part of which they withhold for income tax purposes and hand over once a month to provincial and federal Governments. This Tory Government has now decided to go and get that money twice a month. And during the initial phasing-in period-the result will be the same-because once the system is onstream during the initial implementation year, 1987-1988, they will be getting $1.2 billion more over the fiscal year.
Of course, those $1.2 billion will add up to this Tory administration's actual deficit, which will then go up from $29.3 billion to $30.5 billion. Those are the facts. After three years of Tory administration, after an economic recovery that has been going on since 1983, after increasing taxes by $22 billion on the backs of Canadian taxpayers, they now have come up with a $30.5 billion deficit. And is that the last trick used to arrive at that deficit figure? No, there is yet another one. There is the $1.2 billion windfall. There is the deferral of a $200 million expenditure with regard to the Department of National Defence. Another tricky way of saying: We will spend those dollars but we will not pay them out-we will wait until next year. And this means they are adding to the deficit. This is another $200 million to be added to the deficit figure. And, finally, in the envelope-since they changed cash management methods with respect to the envelope for public assistance to development, they succeeded again in coming up with an artificial saving of $150 million for this year only. All this means, Madam Speaker, that without handling anything, simply by presenting figures on the same basis as in previous years-because clearly, changing the accounting basis alters the basis for comparison-the actual deficit for fiscal year 1987-88 amounts to $30.8 billion, even before making provision as the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) has himself stated for the ice-breaker that was announced with great fanfare by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) last week.

March 9, 1987
Borrowing Authority
There is no provision nor estimates either for implementing the Prime Minister's commitment with respect to child care programs. There is no money either provided for the anti-drug action referred to by the Prime Minister and the Minister for social affairs in their speeches. There is no provision for that.
We have no reservation either against granting assistance to western farmers who in 1988 will probably face the same conditions as in 1987 with respect to wheat price and the Government had earmarked therefor $1 billion which means, Madam Speaker, that the Minister of Finance and the Government are trying to tinker with the books. Actually, the 1987-88 deficit will exceed $29.3 billion and it already does as a result of tricks used by the Minister, but if we take into consideration all those commitments made since the Budget Speech for which no estimate has been provided, the deficit will be considerably higher. This is the reason why the Government was wise enough to cover up because when a Bill is introduced asking the House the authority to borrow, since the money can be used for almost any purpose and allotted to any department, the debate deals almost entirely with public administration. In order to avoid that, the Minister have resorted to a double dodge. He said: Since we are in March, today being March 9, we will earmark $3 billion for the period ending March 3l'
1987,	and another $3 billion as a reserve for up to the end of
1988.	This means that the Minister of Finance has arranged for some room to manoeuvre ranging between $3 and $5 billion so that he would be in a position to borrow further amounts without having to come back to the House and face another public debate and relevant questions. We have before us the first instalment, the first $3.6 billion which will be used to repay the loans made by the Minister of Finance to protect the Canadian dollar on the exchange market.
Madam Speaker, I wonder why a Government which would like to see the interest rates decrease-this is at least what the Minister has said, although he has maintained that there is no magic formula . . . Last year when the dollar was dropping I asked the Minister what he intented to do. He told us that he had no control over interest rates and the dollar value. In his Budget, he congratulated his Government for having succeeded in reducing interest rates. He cannot of course have his cake and it eat too and cannot say when conditions are bad that interest rates are controlled by the United States and that the markets are controlling the value of the Canadian dollar, and take credit when conditions are better. I think that the Minister would do well to correct his statements and remain consistent in his comments .
However, more recently it has been suggested that up to $3.6 billion should be borrowed to avoid an overvaluation of the Canadian dollar. Madam Speaker, there is now a gap in interest rates between Canada and the United States on 90-day Treasury Bills-or at least there was up to last week-end- of between 130 and 140 percentage points, that is to say, between 1.3 per cent and 1.4 per cent. I wonder if, instead of overcharging the loans, the policy of the Department of Finance should not be rather directed toward lowering interest
rates, in view of the fact that the Canadian dollar, under pressure from the market, is somewhat stronger. I wonder why the Government is artificially maintaining interest rates at that level, when it could easily reduce the gap by, say, as much as 50 percentage points, thereby making it possible for Canadian men and women to benefit from this situation, instead of fighting against foreign speculators who, under pressure from the United States for a devaluation of the American dollar, are taking refuge in Canada and buying Treasury bills and other Canadian securities because the funds available to them must be invested somewhere and I do not see why the Minister of Finance is so anxious to take these so-called speculators, to tax instead of allowing interest rates to go down a little as a result of the current gap. I imagine $3.6 billion amount being sought could have been lower. I have already mentioned of course with regard to the forecast deficit, the $3 billion reserve.
As I stated a while ago, Madam Speaker to reflect facts without decieving Canadian men and women the real deficit for fiscal year 1987-88, should have been estimated at $30,850 billion. But when we consider the other moves made by this Government, we realize that part of its deficit has been transferred to the provinces and municipalities in the following ways:
Let us begin with municipalities. Municipalities table their budget once a year, as we all know, and their budget must balance. By changing sales taxes, by widening the sales tax base to include components of asphalt and prestressed materials, concrete, etc., we have transferred to municipalities an additional charge which forces them to either curtail their services or raise their taxes. We have in fact transferred part of the deficit to municipalities by forcing them to pay to the Federal Government taxes which they did not pay before. Secondly, by also raising the tax on gasoline-an input which is of course used by public utilities, transport commissions, etc., bus and subway services-we have added to the financial burden of municipalities. The deficit has been shifted in part from the federal Government to the municipalities.
This is even truer and more striking in the case of provincial Governments. 1 have mentioned this before in the House, but 1 would simply like to recall the impact of the federal Government's decision to curtail transfer payments to finance health programs such as hospital insurance and medicare, as well as post-secondary education, a program so essential that it bears repeating and one which cannot be turned on and off like water from a tap. No act or ministerial decision can regulate the number of people who are ill or will suffer health problems in a province, whether in Quebec, Ontario, New Brunswick or British Columbia. Provincial autorities who are responsible for the administration of hospitals, health care and post-secondary education are faced with the urgent needs of users. At a time when provinces were making considerable efforts to control their expenditures, the federal Government decided proprio motu after offhandedly notifying the provinces of its decision,
March 9, 1987

to reduce by 2 per cent the growth rate of federal transfers for the funding of those programs. What it means is that, instead of sharing in the evolving growth of collective wealth, the Gross National Product, it was decided transfer payments would be geared to the Gross National Product less 2 per cent.
Madam Speaker, according to figures that are quite precise even though they are preliminary, that represents a deficit transfer from the federal to the provincial Governments of about $8 billion, give or take a few billions, in the next five years.
That amounts to $2 billion for the Province of Quebec and about the same for the Province of Ontario. The federal deficit has simply been shifted to the deficit of the provinces. Then they boast that financial positions have been substantially improved. Madam Speaker, if the financial statements of Canada were presented on a comparative and real basis, we would realize that after three or four years of economic recovery, after tax increases of billions of dollars, the deficit the federal Government made one of its top priorities after the election is at the same level if not higher than in the last full year of the Liberal administration.
Madam Speaker, this Government has transferred part of its deficit onto the provinces and their taxpayers, from British Columbia to Newfoundland. There is no exception, all Canadians provinces will have to share this loss of $8 billion. Maybe the Hon. Member disagrees with the decision made by his Government. He should say so. The figures agreed upon during the federal-provincial conferences on the subject show that between 1987 and 1991, that is the next five years, there will be a transfer of $8 billion. In other words, the federal Government will contribute $8 billion less to Medicare, hopital insurance and post-secondary education.
Who is going to pay? Are we going to forbid people from being sick? Are we going to deny a college or university education to our young people? Is that what we are going to do? Are we going to ask families to contribute more substantially to the cost of education in CEGEPs in Quebec, colleges in other provinces and universities? Unless the Government asks or forces the provinces to eliminate some services? That is-during the weekend, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Vincent) was on a radio program, and I heard him say that he had no reason to believe that provinces should spend that much money. I hope he is the only one in his group to think that way and that Hon. Members from all provinces are aware of the importance of postsecondary education, aware of the importance of Hospital Insurance and Medicare, especially for an aging population, and will not echo this rubbish from the Parliamentary Secretary who says that Quebec, Ontario and the other provinces can merrily cut into the financing of their hospital insurance, Medicare and especially post-secondary education programs.
This Conservative Government has transferred part of the deficit to the provinces in order to reduce somewhat the debt and the borrowing it will have to do-without that the amount
Borrowing Authority
in Bill C-40 would be higher-and, now, the Ministers of Finance in Ontario, Quebec and the other provinces will have to go and borrow on the financial markets instead of this Minister.
But also there were drastic changes made in equalization payments. Madam Speaker, the equalization formula was changed in 1982. It is true. The purpose was to extend the base for arriving at the average for comparison purposes. And since in that equalization formula, agreed upon in 1982 by all provinces and the Government of Canada, there was a danger that the new formula would not bring about the same results as the former formula, the then Canadian Government had guaranteed that the payments made under the new formula would not be lower than those granted under the previous one. And as evidence of its good faith, the federal Government said: We will guarantee that for three years. Because it was felt at that time by everyone, the technicians included, and it was actually believed that that was going to happen. Unfortunately, the projections proved to be worse than had been foreseen, and after three years, a correction had to be made, because the guaranteeing formula had operated for three years and as it was coming to an end, a correction had to be made.
Madam Speaker, that correction was made. That is true. Except that, in usual Tory fashion, an injustice was produced that I have been denouncing in this House since the impact is known. The then Minister of State (Finance) had stated from her seat, speaking on behalf of the Government, that each province would receive in equalization payments at least 95 per cent of the money it had received the previous year. The additional money that were voted by this House ensured that all provinces got at least 95 per cent with one exception, Quebec. Why those double standards? Why did the Government refuse and still refuses to honour its promise and the commitment made in this House by the Minister of State (Finance)? Why impose on Quebec taxpayers alone the burden of levying or paying those $66 million that have increased to nearly $90 million?
Why that discrimination against one single province? Madam Speaker, if such commitment had been made by the Parliamentary Secretary or by a back-bencher it would be understandable, but it was actually made in this House by someone in the Government. We thus see that this Government not only reneges on its election commitments but then it does not even honour the commitments made in this House by a Minister answering from his seat on its behalf to a question put by the Opposition. If those commitments had been honoured and part of the deficit had not been transferred to the provincial Governments through the financing of established programs, if such firm commitments made to the provinces had been kept, we would see that the management of the public debt and the deficit by the Conservative Government is far less wonderful than what the Minister of Finance and other Government Members would like to have us believe in their comments inside and outside this House.

Borrowing Authority
Bill C-40 is an example of how the Government mismanages public funds. The Minister of Finance has used a number of tricks to camouflage part of his borrowing. He asks to borrow $3.6 billion for his operations in order to maintain the value of the Canadian dollar. He asks for another $24.3 billion for regular government operations. He asks for an additional $3 billion just in case.
I suppose the additional $3 billion for the end of the year could not cover the commitments made by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) with respect to building an icebreaker, since there is nothing in the Estimates to finance even part of it. Will this additional $3 billion be used to finance the day care system announced by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) last Monday? Or will it be used to cover the expenses of other programs which have been announced by different Ministers and for which there are no figures provided in the Estimates? If this is so, then the deficit for fiscal year 1987-88 will not be $29 billion but something closer to $34 billion. We know that the real deficit is higher than the one contained in the Budget Speech.
The Minister has used a number of tricks to hide certain expenses. We know that he transferred a part of the deficit to the provinces as a result of changes in the way the Established Program Financing arrangements are financed and also as a result of changes that have been made to the equalization formula by the Government.
We realize that the Government has not lived up to its promises. We heard members of the Government make a number of promises during the election campaign. In the House and outside the House we have heard the Minister of Finance say that he will never increase taxes. Yet we know that he has increased taxes by billions and billions of dollars. It is unbelievable that a Government can so openly deny all its commitments and then bring down a Bill such as this, which is similar to the one passed in 1985-86 and which will add thousands of dollars on to the shoulders of Canadians. That is the increase per worker in the national debt under the Tory Government.
These are good reasons for the Official Opposition to say that we intend to vote against the Bill. In doing so we will ask the Government to live up to its promises. The Government promised a certain number of things to Canadian taxpayers. We realize day after day that the promises are broken day after day. In voting against Bill C-40 we send an additional message to the Government to be responsible and to live up to its promises.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1986-87 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, i wish to participate in this debate on Bill C-40 more out of a sense of sorrow than out of a sense of anger, since it effectively continues some of the concerns which my Party has raised in the course of the debate on the Budget. I appreciate the courtesy of the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Hockin) in
March 9, 1987
giving us some insight before the Bill was brought forward. We have had some discussions with him about the purposes of the Bill that was brought forward in terms of borrowing for the exchange fund and in meeting the Government's budget borrowing requirements as a consequence of the deficit forecast and the cash requirements of the 1987 Budget. I also appreciate that some self-interest was involved on the part of the Government because there is a deadline with respect to this Bill. Its passage is required by the end of the month, and the Minister was seeking to have some co-operation from opposition critics.
Co-operation does not necessarily mean support. We in the New Democratic Party remain concerned about the failure of the Government to take any meaningful action with respect to regional disparities in Canada in the course of the Budget. Of course, this borrowing Bill does not hit at that directly but it certainly hits at it indirectly. It speaks to a recipe for deficit reduction which people in my Party find uncomfortable and unacceptable to live with.
In terms of deficit reduction the Government's view seems to be that deficits can be reduced in two ways. Taxes can be increased, particularly those on individuals, and that has been done with a vengeance. Since the Government came to power revenues from personal and sales taxes have increased by more than 50 per cent at the same time that revenues from the corporate sector, in terms of taxation, have actually gone down. Taxes on individuals can be increased in order to combat the deficit, or programs can be cut back. The Government can cut back on its Canadian Jobs Strategy, for example, something which directly affects disadvantaged Canadians. These are people who are out of a job and who need assistance in getting back into the labour force or who need assistance in terms of obtaining training for the new skills that are required in the 1980s and the 1990s. The Government can cut back on spending in economic and regional development, as it has done with a vengeance since taking power. Or it can cut back on the programs of the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion, as it has also done since taking power.
In other words-

-the Government's economic policy for getting rid, of the deficit is either to increase taxes that affect us personally, such as sales tax, or cutting Government spending, and especially spending that affects individuals such as job creation, the Department of Employment and Immigration's job strategy and the regional industrial expansion programs in the Government's Budget.
That is their policy. However, Madam Speaker, there is no concern about the need for a full employment policy, the need for getting rid of the unemployment that unfortunately still exists in our country. The Budget offers nothing in this respect, and in fact, Bill C-40 merely reflects the Budget as far as unemployment is concerned in this country. In fact, the Government is saying we will have to accept the employment
March 9, 1987

situation, instead of setting goals for reducing unemployment, just as the Government sets goals every year to reduce the deficit.
Madam Speaker, I would like to quote from a speech given last Friday by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) at the Macdonald-Cartier Club in Calgary, which was about the Government's policy, not just how it affects the West, but the Government's policy in general.
We know to what extent the vacuum in terms of leadership in the Government has allowed power to drift back into the Department of Finance. We also know what happened when the present Minister took over the Department of Finance two and a half years ago. He was one of the few Ministers to still be in the same position two and a half years after the Government came to power. He found a group of advisers who were, relatively speaking, of like mind with the Hon. Minister. They are increasingly taking charge of the Government.
You may recall, Madam Speaker, because you were a candidate in that election, how the Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) promised that there would be jobs, jobs, jobs immediately the Conservative Government came to power. For example, in the Province of Quebec there is still an unemployment rate of over 11 per cent in the city and region of Montreal, one of the two metropolises of our country.
After two and half years, that is not good enough, but that is the result that we have had from the Government, and from the policies put forward by the Minister of Finance. These policies reflect a wing of policy of his Party. 1 also believe that they reflect the views of the business community in Canada, and the traditional views which have been put forward by the Department of Finance for many years. At times they win, at times they lose. Now they are on a roll because of the disbandment by a Leader of the Opposition, when he was Prime Minister, of the ministry responsible for economic development, because of disbanding and other efforts to balance the control and direction of economic policies within the Government, and because of the fact that the Department of Finance has therefore become much more powerful than it was two or three years ago.
In Calgary on Friday, in the conclusion to his speech to the Macdonald-Cartier Club, the Minister of Finance said this, "In my remarks today, I have stressed the fact that the government you elected," and "you" is underlined, "in September, 1984, has carried out your program," "your" is underlined, "your desires for fiscal rejuvenation", "your" is underlined, "your principles of a market-driven economy," "your" is underlined, "and your commitment to stimulating the private sector." "Your" is also underlined. I would challenge any Conservative, including Conservatives from Calgary, to tell me that there was a large group of unemployed Calgarians or Albertans who were in the hall of the Macdonald-Cartier Club when that meeting was held on Friday;
Borrowing Authority
that there were a great many single mothers who are on welfare; a large number of native people; a large number of handicapped people; a large number of poor people. Were they in that hall? No, they were not. The people who were in that hall were representatives of the business community in Alberta who came together to hear the Minister of Finance.
I recognize that a serious downturn has occurred in the Alberta economy because of changes in the energy sector. This has affected the business community, as well as other people in the population of the Province of Alberta. My Party has also recognized that in calling for specific action. My Leader has been calling for specific action to take the revenue from the increase in taxation on gasoline and use it for the small producers of oil and gas who have been shut out by the Government's policies of catering to the large producers and the multinationals, and not to the small producers.
What is interesting is the blatant, unabashed, and unashamed manner in which the Minister of Finance said to the representatives of the business community that we are following "your program, your desires for fiscal rejuvenation"-that means cut the deficit before other priorities-"your principles of a market-driven economy, and your commitment to stimulating the private sector".
Over the weekend I refreshed my memory of what has been occurring in politics over the last decade or so in terms of the dying years of the Trudeau Government in its first and second manifestations, the brief blip when the Conservatives were in power under the Right Hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark), and now under the Government of the present Prime Minister. The point that was made in an excellent book which I recommend to all Members of Parliament, Ron Graham's book, One-Eyed Kings, is that there has been in the past something of an accommodation in terms of Government policy between accommodating the interests of the business elite in the country on the one hand, and also ensuring an adequate policy in terms of job creation, and in terms of a net of welfare services for average Canadians. That was followed under previous governments, often because of the efforts and pressures of the New Democratic Party.
A Government to stay in power, if it is one of the two old Parties, has probably no choice but to try to balance the needs of ordinary Canadians, and accommodate its friends in the business elite. I say quite bluntly that what has happened is that the policies that are reflected in Bill C-40, and are reflected in the Budget, are policies which are designed to accommodate the business elite and ignore the needs of ordinary Canadians. That is one of the reasons the Conservatives have fallen to the abysmal levels in terms of public esteem. It is not only that they violated public trust, although that is an extremely important factor, it is that they have violated the trust ofthe people in expecting the next Government of Canada to be implementing its promises of jobs, jobs, jobs in every region of Canada, and to be demonstrating fairness to every Canadian in terms of job creation and in

March 9, 1987
Borrowing Authority
terms of the tax system. These are things which the Government has failed to do.
I wish to cite a few points made by the Minister of Finance in his speech, and then comment on them. In his speech to the business elite in Calgary, he said that he believed "we"- whoever that is-"share a common purpose-that is to restore the economic health throughout this country". Every Party talks about restoring economic health throughout this country. We, as a Party, believe that this is not a matter for rhetoric, it is a matter for action.
When you look at the fact that between January, 1986, and January, 1987, of the net creation of 137,000 jobs across Canada, all but 5,000 of those new jobs were in the Province of Ontario, mostly in southern Ontario, and there were only 5,000 new jobs created in net terms between Newfoundland on the East Coast and British Columbia on the West Coast, I ask what type of restoration of economic health does that amount to? The answer is damn little.
The Minister of Finance stated, and I quote:
I recognize that some regions in this country have not participated fully in the economic recovery, and that a good deal of the growth has been concentrated in other parts of Canada, besides Alberta.
The Minister of Finance euphemistically ignored the fact that today the unemployment rate in seven provinces in Canada is higher than it was at the height of the 1981-82 depression. It is higher in two provinces than it was in September of 1984 when the Conservatives came to power. There has been a certain amount of progress in most provinces since 1984. There has been some reduction in unemployment. But one has to ask if that reduction has been enough. 1 would certainly answer, as I think most Canadians would answer that it has definitely not been enough.
1 wish to cite some figures, and I do not wish to repeat my comments in the Budget debate, but in January of this year unemployment, on a seasonally-adjusted basis, rose again to 9.7 per cent from 9.4 per cent.
As we pointed out-

-in seven provinces, the unemployment rate today is higher than it was during the 1981-82 recession. If we consider two of our provinces, Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia, the unemployment rate is higher today than it was in September 1984. Madam Speaker, if we look at the situation in our major cities, we find the following: According to Statistics Canada, in January the unemployment rate was 15 per cent in Vancouver, the Expo '86 city; in Victoria, the capital of British Columbia, it was 14.6 per cent; in Edmonton, 12.5 per cent; in Saskatoon,
11.4 per cent; in Montreal, the metropolis of the Province of Quebec, the unemployment rate, according to the Parliamentary Secretary, was 11.4 per cent, while it was 10.3 per cent in Quebec City. In St. John's, Halifax and Saint John, unemployment was 10.8, 10.4 and 12.1 percent respectively.
Such is the difficult situation in our major cities, and you know quite well, Madam Speaker, that unemployment is often much higher in rural areas than in major cities.
If we compare this with the situation in Toronto, where the constituency of the Minister of Finance, Etobicoke, is located, we find an unemployment rate of 4.8 percent. I am well aware that there are unemployed workers in the Maritimes who spend two or three months working for the building industry in Toronto and that it is difficult to find workers in that city, where the situation approaches what could be called full employment. My son, who is 20 or 21 years old, now works in Toronto, where he has just found a job. It is not a very big job, but there are still jobs in the Toronto area.
However, saving Toronto and the economy of southern Ontario is not the same as saving the economy of the whole country. The Minister of Finance has said that the regions of this country have not participated fully in economic recovery and that much of the growth which has been concentrated in other regions of Canada has failed to occur in Alberta. He is speaking the truth since the major part of this growth has occurred in Ontario.
Madam Speaker, the Minister of Finance has said in his Calgary speech: "We, as national Government, must look at the problems in each region. And I can assure you that we are working and will continue to work night and day to guarantee that all Canadian men and women benefit from the economic resurgence in our country."
Madam Speaker, I have to ask: Where is the economic resurgence in Newfoundland? Where is the economic resurgence in Alberta? In British Columbia? It is not there.
Madam Speaker, the Minister of Finance has also assured us that tax reform is on the fast track. This means that it is being prepared quickly, Madam Speaker. According to the Minister, his proposals will be published in the spring. He says that the Government wants to lower rates and to enlarge the tax base for personal and sales taxes and to reduce the number of tax categories.
However, Madam Speaker, the tone of the speech made by the Minister of Finance suggests that he now expects to achieve neutrality in terms of income, but only for personal and sales taxes. This means that there will be no transfer of the tax burden from individuals to corporations.
If we look at the situation in the United States, Madam Speaker, we find that Congress has just passed a tax reform project to transfer about $132 billion in taxes from individuals to corporations. What is the Minister of Finance saying? He says: "We know that unfair distortions remain in the corporate taxation system. We want to correct promptly-" Madam Speaker, the Government has been in power for two and a half years and it now promises changes and tax reforms although corporate taxes decreased since 1984. But I say that we want to correct promptly those distortions.
March 9, 1987

"Corporate tax rates", he says, "must be lowered to remain competitive in view of tax reforms taking place in the United States."
Madam Speaker, in the United States, taxes paid by corporations have increased by SI32 billion and here is our Minister of Finance saying that in spite of all the tax breaks given to corporations, their tax burden should not be increased at all and that corporate taxes will be lowered.
The Minister says that we will in effect eliminate some loopholes. That is a good thing. But we must also take into account the fact that corporate income tax has not increased at all, while personal income tax have gone up by 50 per cent.
Finally, Madam Speaker, the Minister said to journalists, before the Macdonald-Cartier Club in Calgary, probably answering a question about Petro-Canada: "We believe", he said, "that Petro-Canada has outlived its public policy purpose. Therefore the Government can now proceed to the sale of Petro-Canada."
Madam Speaker, a few Conservative Members agree to the privatization of Petro-Canada. As a New Democrat Member, I can say that the reasons for the purchase of Petro-Canada are still valid, that the Canadian people supported it when it was recommended-on whose suggestion? By a New Democrat under the minority Government of 1972-74. One of the reasons why New Democrats are now on an equal footing with Liberals in the Province of Quebec is because we, the NDP, recognize why Canadians wish to maintain Petro-Canada as a Crown corporation.
I am very concerned to hear Conservatives in the Flouse supporting the perhaps offhand comments made by the Minister of Finance in Calgary, suggesting that Petro-Canada no longer fulfilled any public policy role and therefore we could move ahead in order to sell it off. We think there is a public role. We think the Government should have directed Petro-Canada in the last two weeks not to go along with the increase in gasoline prices which was put into place by one of the multinational oil companies. We think-and Canadians think it as well-that one of the reasons for Petro-Canada is to have a window on the industry and to have a means by which to protect Canadians from being gouged at the petrol pumps by private multinational corporations. That was the situation which prevailed back in the 1970s. We feel-I think most Canadians feel it-we do not want to see a situation where we are once again held to ransom by privately owned oil companies if energy prices start to climb in a dizzying spiral, as they did at that time.
The Minister of Finance also talked about how he viewed the world. In speaking to a business audience-and there were certainly no poor people there-he said that the deregulation of industry in an approved climate to foster entrepreneurship and attract foreign investment and freer trade was part of the

fundamental belief that the best economic decisions are those which are made in the market-place.

speechtext:
Again Conservative Members are saying: "Hear, hear", as they listen to me quoting certain comments of the Minister of Finance.
The other day I rose in the House to ask the Minister of Finance why it was the Government, which has fallen over itself in order to try to attract foreign investment and show that Canada is "open for business again", in their words, had in fact done so badly. In 1985 and 1986 combined we had a net outflow of some $10 billion on job creating-the long term direct investment account. Direct investment by Canadians, Madam Speaker, accounted for a $10 billion outflow over those two years, $5.1 billion in 1985 and $4.8 billion in 1986.
What happened in terms of direct investment from foreigners? Direct investment by foreigners was up by $1.5 billion in 1986 but it had fallen by $2.5 billion the previous year. So over those two years Canada had a direct investment outflow, a disinvestment by foreigners of more than $1 billion. Yet the Finance Minister goes to Calgary and says "Look what a great job we are doing in attracting direct investment from foreigners". But he and the Government are doing a lousy job.
One of the miracles that was going to happen for the economy was that money would come flowing in in direct investment to help create jobs, particularly in the depressed regions of Canada, but that did not occur at all. In fact, the direct opposite occurred. American multinational corporations have been pulling investment out of Canada. We are seeing this even in the industrial heartland of Ontario. In the riding of my leader, Oshawa, in the chocolate factory, which has employed 400 people, a rationalization is taking place. Is it the Roundtree plant that is closing, it has been taken over by Cadbury's-perhaps it is the other way around-
